verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern across Torah, Prophets, Writings, Gospel, and Epistle converges on corruption that reaches every named faculty of fallen man and on a denied capacity to come to God unaided. Genesis 6:5 stacks the universal and restrictive quantifiers (words for 'every' and 'only'): 'every' (kol) 'formed-purpose' (yetser) 'of the thoughts' (machshevot) 'of his heart' (libbo) was 'only' (raq) 'evil' (ra) 'all' (kol) 'the day' (hayyom), queried and confirmed as the token sequence H4284 H3820A H3605 H7535 H3336 H7451 in the store. Jeremiah 17:9 predicates the 'heart' (leb) as 'deceitful' (aqob, H6121A, a term occurring only 3 times in the canon) 'more than all' (min kol) and 'incurably sick' (anush, H0605), closing with the interrogative-pronoun clause 'who can know it' (mi yedaennu) (a BHSA XYqt clause, IPrP subject, that is a clause where the question-word 'who' fills the subject slot) that functions as universal negation. Romans 3:10 to 18 assembles a catena (a chain of stitched-together quotations) whose Greek reads 'there is none righteous, not even one' (ouk estin dikaios oude heis), twin negated participles 'the one understanding' (ho synion) and 'the one seeking God' (ho ekzeton ton theon), 'all turned aside' (pantes exeklinan), the once-occurring verb 'they became useless' (echreothesan), and 'there is none, not as far as one' (ouk estin heos henos), then enumerates throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, and eyes. Ephesians 2:1 to 3 predicates 'being dead' (nekrous ontas) (a present participle of state, meaning ongoing settled condition) and 'children by nature of wrath' (tekna physei orges). Romans 8:7 to 8, John 6:44, and 1 Corinthians 2:14 deny capacity at verb modality with 'it is not able' (ou dynatai) and 'no one is able' (oudeis dynatai). The one underdetermined point is the SCOPE word total: the vocabulary establishes extensive reach across faculties but does not by itself rank extensive-totality against prevailing-but-not-absolute corruption, so a fair lens range is recorded.

scripture.reasoning: Queried token sequence in the store is H4284 'thoughts' (machshevot), H3820A 'heart' (leb), H3605 'every' (kol), H3117 'day' (yom), then H7535 'only' (raq), H3336 'formed purpose' (yetser), and H3605 'all' (kol) again with H7451 'evil' (ra) doubled. The clause 'every formed purpose of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day' (kol yetser machshevot libbo raq ra kol-hayyom) reads as such in English. The universal quantifier 'every' (kol) brackets the clause twice and the restrictive 'only' (raq) excludes a non-evil remainder. Note that 'only' (raq) and 'every' (kol) co-occur in 37 verses across the canon, so they are ordinary restrictive and universal particles; their force here is set by the saturating stack, not by a rare word.

Queried sequence includes H3336 'formed purpose' (yetser), H3068 'the LORD' (YHWH), H3820A 'heart' (leb), the same 'heart' word again, and H7451 'evil' (ra) with 'from his youth' (mineurav). The clause 'the formed purpose of the human heart is evil from youth' (yetser leb haadam ra mineurav) declares the formed purpose of the human heart evil from youth, restating Genesis 6:5 after the flood and grounding the corruption as a constant of the post-fall human heart rather than a one-generation verdict.

Queried token order is H3820A 'heart' (leb), H6121A 'deceitful and twisted' (aqob), H1931 'it' (hu), H3605 'more than all' (kol, with the comparative 'min' prefix meaning 'from/more than'), H4310 'who' (mi), H0605 'incurably sick' (anush), H3045 'know' (yada). BHSA (a syntactic database of the Hebrew Bible) parses three clauses, a nominal clause (a verbless 'X is Y' clause) with PreC (the predicate complement) the adjective 'deceitful' (aqob) and Subj the determined heart, an adjectival clause for 'incurably sick' (anush), and an X-yiqtol clause (a clause where some element comes before the imperfect verb) whose subject is an interrogative pronoun phrase (IPrP, a phrase headed by a question word like 'who'). 'Deceitful' (aqob) occurs only 3 times in the canon and 'incurably sick' (anush) 17 times, clustering in Jeremiah incurable-wound language. The rhetorical 'who can know it' (mi yedaennu) functions as universal negation: no one can fathom the heart.

MorphGNT (a tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'there is none righteous, not even one' (Ouk estin dikaios oude heis). The adverb of negation 'not' (ouk) governs the copula (the linking verb 'is') 'is' (estin), and 'not even one' (oude heis) appends a second negation plus the numeral one to foreclose any exception. Paul opens the catena (the chain of stitched-together quotations) by citing Psalm 14 (which is Psalm 13 in the LXX, the Greek Old Testament known as the Septuagint) language; the store cross-refs Romans 3:10 to Psalm 14:1 and Psalm 53:1.

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms two present-active articular participles (ongoing-action verbal adjectives with the article 'the') each under 'there is not' (ouk estin): 'the one understanding' (ho synion, from the lemma 'to understand' [syniemi]) and 'the one seeking God' (ho ekzeton ton theon, from the lemma 'to seek out' [ekzeteo]). The construction negates the cognitive faculty (understanding) and the volitional faculty (seeking God) in parallel, which is the verse that most directly supports corruption reaching distinct faculties.

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'all turned aside' (pantes exeklinan, with 'all' [pas] in the nominative plural, the subject form) and 'they became useless' (echreothesan, aorist passive third plural, that is, a completed past action in passive voice, from the lemma 'to be made useless' [achreioomai]). A grep of all MorphGNT files confirms 'to be made useless' (achreioomai) occurs exactly once in the New Testament, so it is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) whose sense, rendered useless or made worthless, is fixed by its Psalm 14 (in the LXX, the Greek Old Testament) source rather than triangulated from other New Testament uses. The verse closes with 'there is none doing good, there is none, not as far as one' (ouk estin ho poion chrestoteta, ouk estin heos henos).

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'their throat is an open grave' (taphos aneogmenos ho larynx auton), 'they kept deceiving' (edoliousan, from the lemma 'to deceive' [dolioo]), and 'poison of asps under their lips' (ios aspidon hypo ta cheile auton). The speech organs throat, tongue, and lips are figured as instruments of death and deceit, extending the indictment to the bodily faculty of speech. The store cross-refs Romans 3:13 to Psalm 5:9 and Psalm 140:3.

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'there is no fear of God before their eyes' (ouk estin phobos theou apenanti ton ophthalmon auton). This caps the catena (the chain of stitched-together quotations) by negating the affective and reverential faculty, the fear of God, and locating the lack at the eyes. The store cross-refs Romans 3:18 to Psalm 36:1.

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'being dead in the trespasses and the sins' (ontas nekrous tois paraptomasin kai tais hamartiais). The participle 'being' (ontas) is present of 'to be' (eimi), a state predicate, not an event, so death is the standing condition of the unregenerate rather than a process they undergo. The store cross-refs Ephesians 2:1 to Colossians 2:13 and to Romans 3:10, linking the death image to the catena (the chain of stitched-together quotations).

MorphGNT (the tagged Greek New Testament dataset) confirms 'we all conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts' (hemeis pantes anestraphemen pote en tais epithymiais tes sarkos hemon, poiountes ta thelemata tes sarkos kai ton dianoion). The pairing 'flesh' (sarx) plus 'thought, understanding' (dianoia) couples bodily appetite with cognition. The clause closes 'and we were by nature children of wrath' (kai emetha tekna physei orges); 'by nature' (physei) is a dative of respect (the 'to/by/with' grammatical form indicating respect or manner), and 'nature' (physis) is the strongest lexical anchor for corruption as constitutive nature, the same word the minority lens contests.

'The mindset of the flesh is enmity toward God, for it does not submit to the law of God, neither indeed is it able' (To phronema tes sarkos echthra eis theon, to gar nomo tou theou ouch hypotassetai, oude gar dynatai). 'Mindset' (phronema) is the cognitive disposition; 'it is not able' (ou dynatai) is a present indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) absolute denial of capacity, not a denial of permission. The store cross-refs Romans 8:7 to Jeremiah 13:23 (can the leopard change its spots) and to 1 Corinthians 2:14.

'Those who are in the flesh are not able to please God' (Hoi de en sarki ontes theo aresai ou dynantai). The articular participle 'being' (ontes, the participle 'being' with the article 'the') marks a constitutive state of being in the flesh, and 'they are not able' (ou dynantai) is a categorical denial of capacity. The verb 'to be able' (dynamai) is the semantic hinge that ties the depravity verdict to inability rather than mere disinclination.

'No one is able to come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him' (Oudeis dynatai elthein pros me ean me ho pater ho pempsas me helkyse auton). 'No one is able' (oudeis dynatai) is an absolute negation of capacity confirmed in the store at this verse, and the 'unless' (ean me) clause sets prior divine drawing ('to draw' [helkyo]) as the necessary condition. The store cross-refs John 6:44 to John 12:32, Jeremiah 13:23, and Jeremiah 31:3.

'The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he is not able to know them' (Psychikos de anthropos ou dechetai ta tou pneumatos tou theou, moria gar auto estin, kai ou dynatai gnonai). 'He does not receive' (ou dechetai) negates reception and 'he is not able to know' (ou dynatai gnonai) negates the cognitive faculty of knowing spiritual things, pairing will and mind.

complicating_texts.resolution: God saw all that he had made, 'behold, very good' (hinneh tov meod). This is the pre-fall creational verdict and is cross-referenced from Romans 3:12 in the bundle precisely as the contrast. It does not complicate the verdict because the proposition concerns FALLEN man; the Genesis 6:5 and Genesis 8:21 corruption clauses are post-fall and use 'evil formed purpose of heart' (yetser leb ra) to mark the change.

God made 'humanity upright' (adam yashar) but they sought 'many devices' (hishshebonot rabbim). The verse fixes original uprightness as the prior state and present universal departure as the current one, which is consistent with the post-fall depravity verdict rather than against it.

Gentiles 'by nature do the things of the law' (physei ta tou nomou poiosin) shows residual moral awareness, but Romans 2:15 says their reasonings either accuse or excuse, and Romans 3:9 concludes 'all under sin' (pantas hyph hamartian). The phrase posits natural conscience, not autonomous saving capacity, so it does not contradict the inability clauses.

'To seek God if perhaps they might grope for him' (zetein ton theon ei ara ge pselapheseian auton) uses the rare optative (a mood expressing wish or remote possibility) 'might grope' (pselapheseian) inside an 'if perhaps' (ei ara ge) clause expressing remote, doubtful possibility. The grammar marks groping in the dark, which underlines incapacity rather than asserting realized ability.

'The true light that enlightens every man' (phos to alethinon ho photizei panta anthropon) speaks of Christ illuminating all, but John 1:10 to 11 immediately says 'the world did not know him' (ho kosmos auton ouk egno) and 'his own did not receive him' (hoi idioi auton ou parelabon), so universal illumination does not entail universal unaided positive response.

variant_units_examined.note: Witnesses read 'they became useless' (echreothesan) or the variant spelling (achreiothesan); the spelling difference does not change the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) lemma 'to be made useless' (achreioomai) or its sense of being rendered useless.

Minor word-order variation between 'trespasses' (paraptomasin) and 'sins' (hamartiais) does not touch the 'being dead' (ontas nekrous) state predicate (a verbless or 'being' clause that names an ongoing condition) that carries the verdict.
Subjunctive 'might draw' (helkyse) versus future 'will draw' (helkysei) does not affect the 'no one is able to come' (oudeis dynatai elthein) negation of capacity.

variants.note: All anchors lie outside the ingested CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a textual-criticism technique for mapping manuscript relationships) 3 John sample (not_in_ecm_scope is true in the bundle). Variant survey rests on apparatus shadow data only (the ECM apparatus is the critical edition of New Testament textual variants); no examined reading shifts the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes the quantifier stack at plain force. Genesis 6:5 brackets the clause with 'every' (kol) twice and 'only' (raq) once, Jeremiah 17:9 says the heart is deceitful 'more than all' (min kol) and incurably sick, Romans 3:11 negates understanding and seeking as separate faculties, Romans 3:13 to 18 enumerates throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, and eyes, and Ephesians 2:3 names flesh, thoughts, and 'nature' (physis). On this reading the canon distributes corruption across each named faculty, and the 'to be able' (dynamai) constructions in Romans 8:7 to 8, John 6:44, and 1 Corinthians 2:14 deny saving capacity at verb modality. The word total is read as extensive (no faculty exempt), not as absolute (man as bad as possible), which the texts also do not assert.

Reaches the same affirmation but treats the quantifiers as marking the dominant and pervasive bent of the heart rather than a clinical claim that every micro-faculty is equally and maximally corrupt. 'Only' (raq) and 'every' (kol) co-occur in 37 verses across the canon as ordinary restrictive and universal particles, so the strength here comes from the saturating context, and this lens reads the catena (the chain of stitched-together Old Testament quotations) and Genesis 6:5 as describing what characteristically rules fallen man while still grounding real inability to please or come to God. The inability verbs 'it is not able' (ou dynatai) and 'no one is able' (oudeis dynatai) are read as decisive even on this milder construal of extent.

Notes that several catena (the chain of stitched-together Old Testament quotations) sources (Psalm 14, Psalm 5, Psalm 10, Psalm 36, Isaiah 59) are covenant-lawsuit or imprecatory poetry where 'there is not' (ouk estin) and 'all' (pantes) language can be hot prophetic rhetoric against a wicked party rather than a flat anthropological universal, and that Hebrew poetic totality terms often function as emphatic hyperbole. On this lens the vocabulary alone does not settle whether corruption is extensive across every faculty or prevailingly described, because the words establish reach but do not rank the two construals. This lens is recorded so a reader holding it sees its strongest form; the engine still lands affirm because Paul himself recontextualizes the psalms in Romans 3:9 and 3:19 as a universal indictment that stops every mouth, and Genesis 8:21 restates the corruption clause as a settled fact about the human heart from youth outside any lawsuit setting.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on plain grammar that holds across construals: stacked negation with 'not even one' (oude heis) and 'not as far as one' (heos henos), present state participles 'being dead' (ontas nekrous) and 'being in the flesh' (en sarki ontes), the dative (the 'to/by/with' grammatical form) 'by nature' (physei), and the modal 'to be able' (dynamai) denials. The only genuinely underdetermined point is the SCOPE sense of total, where extensive-totality and prevailing-corruption readings both affirm and a covenant-lawsuit-rhetoric reading registers the lexical room; that room is recorded honestly rather than smoothed over.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: How extensively has sin affected the faculties of fallen human beings (mind, will, affections, body), and what is the unaided capacity of fallen man to please God or to initiate saving faith?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem uses the loaded label total depravity and asserts every faculty plus inability in one predicate, which maps onto a specific tradition taxonomy and also risks the misreading that total means as-evil-as-possible. The neutralized form separates the extent question from the capacity question and drops the label. The verdict is derived on the original stem and is affirm; the neutral rephrasing is recorded only for transparency. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, affirms is UNCHANGED from the prior evidence file.

lay_summary: The Bible uses a tight cluster of words to describe fallen humanity, and the pattern runs from Genesis through Jeremiah to Paul and John. Genesis 6:5 piles up quantifiers: every formed purpose ('yetser') of the thoughts ('machshevot') of the heart ('leb') was only ('raq') evil ('ra') all the day, with the words for every ('kol'), only ('raq'), and all ('kol') bracketing the clause. Genesis 8:21 repeats it after the flood, the heart is evil from youth, so it reads as a standing fact, not a one-time verdict. Jeremiah 17:9 calls the heart deceitful ('aqob') more than all things and incurably sick ('anush'), then asks who can know it ('mi yedaennu'), a rhetorical question that means no one can. In Romans 3 Paul stacks Old Testament quotations: there is none righteous, not even one ('oude heis'), none who understands ('ho synion'), none who seeks God ('ho ekzeton ton theon'), all have turned aside ('pantes exeklinan'), and a word for became useless ('echreothesan') that appears only once in the whole New Testament. That chain names the throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, and eyes, touching speech, walking, and the absence of any fear of God. Ephesians 2 says the unconverted were being dead ('ontas nekrous') in trespasses ('paraptomasin') and sins ('hamartiais'), using a present participle that marks a settled state, and by nature ('physei') children of wrath, where by nature is the strongest word ('physis') for a built-in condition. Romans 8, John 6:44, and First Corinthians 2:14 then shift from describing corruption to denying capacity, using the verb able ('dynamai') in flat negative form: the fleshly mind cannot ('ou dynatai') submit to God, no one is able ('oudeis dynatai') to come to Christ unless drawn, the natural ('psychikos') person cannot know the things of the Spirit. Where readers can diverge is the exact reach of the word total. The words clearly show corruption touching mind, will, affections, and body, and they clearly deny unaided power to come to God, but the everyday words for all and only do not by themselves rank a claim that every faculty is touched against a claim that corruption prevailingly rules the heart, and some of the quoted psalms are courtroom poetry. Both readings still land on inability, because the verb able is negated outright rather than merely warned against.

The BHSA clause-type parse of Jeremiah 17:9 (the nominal, adjectival, and X-yiqtol clauses with the interrogative-pronoun subject) and the MACULA-Greek syntax anchors for the Ephesians 2:1 state predicate and Romans 8:7 clause structure are load-bearing for the faculty-by-faculty and state-predicate observations, so under-citing to keep the file publishable was not chosen.
